title: In Bengal, Non-Veg Is Not a Treat During Durga Puja — It Is Bhog
excerpt: For Bengali families, mutton and hilsa offered to the Goddess on Navami are sacred prasad — a Shakta tradition that stands apart from North India's vegetarian Navratri.
body:
• In Bengal, fish and mutton during Durga Puja are not a break from piety — they are piety itself. The Goddess arrives as a daughter returning home, and the house cooks what it has always cooked.
  • Navami is the traditional day of offering: in bonedi bari households, mutton is cooked as niramish mangsho — without onion and garlic — then offered to the Goddess and distributed as mahaprasad.
  • The Shakta tradition stands apart from North India's satvik Navratri fasting, showing how one festival carries two very different meanings across India.
  • For Bengali families in the US, keeping this tradition means finding hilsa, goat meat and puja bhog at local pujas and Bengali groceries every autumn.

"I am a vegetarian Bengali," she told the priest at the Mudiali Puja pandal in South Kolkata. He had asked if she was Bengali after watching her devotion during Sandhi Puja on Maha Ashtami. The sentence, as NDTV blogger Chandrima S. Bhattacharya writes, took many by surprise — as if Bengal and fish were one word, as if Durga Puja could not be Durga Puja without a piece of mutton on the plate and a silver hilsa on the thali.

And yet the tradition she describes is precise: in Bengal, non-vegetarian food during the festival is not indulgence. It is bhog — the sacred offering.

The daughter comes home

The theology behind the plate is domestic, not ascetic. In Bengal, Maa Durga does not arrive as a guest who must be wrapped in holiness, the writer explains. She comes as a daughter returning to her father's house. You do not put a daughter on a nine-day fast. You cook what the house has always cooked, what the river gave. In the Shakta way of seeing the world, once the offering is placed before the deity, it becomes prasad.

""Vegetarian mutton" The mutton cooked on Navami is niramish mangsho — cooked without onion and garlic."

Navami carries that meaning most clearly. Ashtami is often the quieter, more satvik day: anjali, khichuri, labra. Navami is traditionally the day of the offering — in many bonedi bari, the old aristocratic households of Kolkata, the memory of sacrifice still lives in the kitchen even when the sacrifice itself has become symbolic.

"Vegetarian mutton"

The mutton cooked on Navami is niramish mangsho — cooked without onion and garlic. The logic is exact: in Bengali tradition, onion and garlic are what make everyday cooking "amish" (non-vegetarian), so mutton cooked with ginger, yoghurt and garam masala counts as niramish for the Goddess's plate. As the NDTV piece puts it, "Mutton becomes a vegetarian meal for prasad when cooked without onion and garlic."

The roots run deep. Animal sacrifice, or bali, was historically part of the ninth day of Durga Puja and Kali Puja in Bengal, and the sacrificed animal — cooked without onion and garlic — was considered maha prasad, food blessed by the Supreme Being, according to Mint Lounge's account of the tradition.

Fish has its own geography in the festival. In many families that trace their origins to erstwhile East Bengal, now Bangladesh, a bhog of fish — often hilsa or rui — is offered on Dashami, the festival's last day, Mint Lounge reports. Dashami is traditionally the last day of the hilsa-eating season, so Bengalis send off both fish and Goddess together, saying "ashchhe bochor agar hobe" — till next year.

Two festivals, one Goddess

The contrast with the rest of India is sharp. While much of North and West India observes Navratri with fasting, discipline and a satvik diet — no onion, garlic or meat — Bengal's Durga Puja is a feast. Both honor Goddess Durga, but through different theologies: in the Vaishnav-influenced north she is the divine mother approached through restraint; in Bengal's Shakta tradition she is the daughter welcomed with celebration.

And the vegetarian Bengali at the pandal is not an outsider to any of this. The same week holds niramish mangsho and khichuri-labra-payesh: khichuri heavy with ghee and roasted moong, labra of pumpkin, brinjal and raw banana, luchi, chholar dal with coconut, aloor dum, tomato-khejur chutney, payesh and mishti doi. Community pandals feed thousands with it. "That meal is not a compromise," the blogger writes. "It is the public heart of puja."

Keeping bhog alive abroad

For Bengali families in the United States, this tradition travels in fragments and is reassembled every autumn. The big community pujas — in the Bay Area, New Jersey, Chicago, Dallas — still serve khichuri bhog by the hundreds of plates, and many organize a Navami mutton curry for members. Goat meat is available at halal butchers and Indian groceries; hilsa appears frozen at Bengali grocery stores before puja, often at a premium diaspora families pay without blinking.

There is a version of the thali with mutton on it, and a version without. As the blogger concludes: both are still the same feast.
image_caption: Bhoga served during Durga Puja in West Bengal, where non-vegetarian offerings like mutton are part of the feast.
nri_angle: Bengali-American families reassemble this tradition every autumn at community pujas and Bengali groceries, where khichuri bhog and Navami mutton keep the Shakta meaning of the festival alive abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
